issues.claim: The Google SRE book describes a blameless postmortem as an analysis that looks for the contributing causes of an incident without indicting any individual or team, and that assumes everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. It also explains why this matters: if mistakes are punished, people stop bringing problems to light.
issues.problem: The wording matches my recollection of the 'Blameless Postmortem' section of the SRE book, including 'or team'. The fetched excerpt starts after that section and does not contain it, so the page support cannot be confirmed from the excerpt. The RU text makes the same claim.
issues.suggestedFix: Re-fetch the page and confirm the passage ('without indicting any individual or team', 'good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had', and people not bringing issues to light for fear of punishment). If it is present, keep the paraphrase. Otherwise soften the wording.

issues.claim: Contracts that the consumer states and the provider verifies (consumer-driven contracts) make the consumer's expectations explicit and reveal an incompatible change in the provider's CI instead of in production.
issues.problem: The Fowler excerpt supports consumer-expressed expectations, rapid feedback on the impact of changes, and deprecating contract elements for a period. It does not show the claim that the tests run in the provider's CI or build and catch breaking changes before production. The generator notes say this is the author's own summary of the pattern. The page's URL and title are confirmed.
issues.suggestedFix: Check the full article for the provider-side contract tests and the point about running them in the build. If it is not there, reword to 'give the provider rapid feedback on which consumer expectations a change would break', or present the CI placement as common practice rather than something the article states.

issues.problem: The cited target is a web page of the online SRE book. This is acceptable, but 'docs' or 'article' would match how the site presents it more closely.
issues.suggestedFix: Keep 'book' or change it to 'article'. Either is fine.

issues.claim: Где на самом деле записан контракт между командами и что его проверяет?
issues.problem: The second half of the hint nearly restates step 4 of the reference answer ('where is the contract written down and what checks it'), so it leans toward giving the answer away.

issues.claim: The Kanban Guide describes this idea as explicitly controlling WIP: the team limits the number of started items, which creates a pull system where new work starts only when capacity frees up. It also defines the metrics to rely on: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time, plus a service level expectation as a forecast of cycle time.
issues.problem: The excerpt confirms that the Definition of Workflow requires a definition of how WIP is controlled, plus WIP, cycle time and an SLE of the form '85% of work items will be finished in eight days or less'. It does not show the 'pull system' wording, throughput, or work item age. These are probably in the guide, but the excerpt does not demonstrate them. The RU text makes the same claim.
issues.suggestedFix: Re-fetch the 2025.5 guide and confirm the pull wording and the four flow metrics (WIP, cycle time, work item age, throughput). Cite the exact page https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2025.5/ rather than the redirecting /english/ URL. If anything is missing, narrow the claim to what the guide states.

issues.claim: https://www.scrum.org/resources/kanban-guide-scrum-teams (cited as 'The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams')
issues.problem: The page exists and has the stated title. The excerpt is a landing page that says only that Kanban is a strategy for optimizing flow in Scrum. It supports none of the specific claims about WIP limits, pull, or flow metrics. The question is also about a general lead, not specifically a Scrum team. This link is a weak source for the claims made.
issues.suggestedFix: Either drop this link or replace it with a source that supports the WIP and cycle-time claims, such as the Kanban Guide 2025.5 page itself. If it is kept, state in the explanation what it is cited for, such as combining Kanban practices with Scrum, and do not imply it covers the WIP metrics.

issues.claim: Если число людей не меняется, а начатых задач становится больше, что происходит со временем, которое каждая задача проводит в работе?
issues.problem: The hint almost states the core answer (more WIP means longer time per task), which is the answer hinge, so it is closer to giving the answer away than nudging toward it. The EN hint has the same issue.
issues.suggestedFix: Make it less direct, e.g. 'Сколько времени задача реально делается, а сколько ждёт, пока автор занят другой?', and give the EN hint the equivalent wording.

issues.claim: Start with a limit below the current level (for example, per team or for the review stage)
issues.problem: Classic Kanban practice, and what the guide's emphasis on current WIP suggests, is to start from the current WIP and tighten it. Starting below the current level is defensible but is presented as the rule.
issues.suggestedFix: Say 'Start at or just below the current WIP and tighten it step by step based on the data', and make the same change in RU.
